Guide, 6 min read

A clear page gives the eye one place to start

Good reading layouts decide what comes first, what supports it, and what can wait. Everything below follows from that.

Body text works best at a comfortable size, with a line length people can follow without losing their place. A link should look like one, and inline values such as --space-4 should be easy to tell apart from prose.

Contrast, spacing and scale do most of the design work before color enters.
  • One heading level per idea.
  • Short paragraphs, generous spacing.
  • Captions quieter than the content they describe.

        Rulebook
        The rules every build follows, shown in your current style.
        
  
        
  
        
    
        These ten rules go into the master prompt. Each one is drawn here in your current build, so you can judge the language as a whole. They are my synthesis of common design-system practice and the research on generic-looking AI interfaces, not an official standard.
        

        

    
        RULE 01
        Hierarchy first
        One focal point per screen. Size, weight and position show importance before color does. Remove anything that carries no meaning.
        
      
        SECTION LABEL
        One clear thing to look at
        Supporting text stays quieter, so the eye lands on the heading, then the action.
        

    
        RULE 02
        Type with intent
        One distinctive family or a deliberate pair, never a default stack. A modular scale, three weights at most, lines of 45 to 75 characters.
        
      
        

    
        RULE 03
        Restrained color
        A tinted neutral ramp, one accent for actions, selection and focus, and semantic colors for status. No decorative gradients, and meaning is never carried by color alone.
        
      
        

    
        RULE 04
        Space on a grid
        A 4px base unit and an 8px rhythm. Related items sit closer together than unrelated ones, and each component size has fixed padding.
        
      
        

    
        RULE 05
        Shape and depth
        One radius family scaled by component size. Borders and tonal layers first; shadows only for things that float. Three elevation levels at most.
        
      
        
        
        Level 1
        border only
        
        
        Level 2
        overlay
        
        
        Level 3
        modal
        

    
        RULE 06
        One look per job, every state
        Primary, secondary, tertiary and destructive buttons, each with default, hover, pressed, focus, disabled and loading states. Inputs add an error state.
        
      
        
        
        default

        RULE 07
        One open-source icon library
        One library for the whole product, chosen in the Icons step, so stroke weight and corner style stay consistent. Pair icons with text labels unless the meaning is universal. No hand-drawn icons, no emoji.

        RULE 08
        Motion that explains
        120 to 200 ms for feedback, 200 to 320 ms for transitions. Ease-out when things enter, ease-in when they leave. Motion shows cause and effect, and respects reduced motion.
        
      
        
        
        
        Solid: ease-out (enter). Dashed: ease-in (leave).
        

    
        RULE 09
        Plain, human voice
        Short and specific. Buttons name the action. Errors say what happened and what to do next. Real content, never lorem ipsum or placeholder names.

        RULE 10
        Accessible by construction
        Text at 4.5:1, interface parts at 3:1, a visible focus ring, 44px touch targets, a full keyboard path. These readouts are computed from the tokens you chose.
        
      
        
  
        
    
        
    
        Style should never fight usability. The prompts ask the AI to audit against Nielsen's 10 heuristics, as published by Nielsen Norman Group, and to rate each problem on NN/G's 0 to 4 severity scale. The style translation under each one is this tool's own addition.
        
      
        

        
    
        0Not a usability problem at all.
        
    
        1Cosmetic only. Fix if there is spare time.
        
    
        2Minor usability problem. Low priority.
        
    
        3Major problem. Important to fix.
        
    
        4Usability catastrophe. Fix before release.
        
  
        
  
        
    
        Severity has three parts. How often it happens, how hard it is to overcome, and whether it keeps bothering people (frequency, impact, persistence).
        
    
        One rater is not enough. NN/G reports ratings from a single evaluator are unreliable. Run the audit two or three times and compare.
        
    
        It is a first pass. A heuristic review finds obvious problems cheaply. Confirm with real people using the five test tasks the prompt asks for.
        
  
        
    
        
    
        Research on generic-looking AI interfaces points to process and context, not cleverer wording. NN/G also found that vague prompts produced cluttered, inconsistent layouts.
        
      
        
        
        The "made by AI" tells
          
          
        • Default type: Inter, Roboto or a system stack with no decision behind it.
          • 
          
        • Purple-to-blue gradients and gradient text.
          • 
          
        • Centered hero plus three icon cards as the answer to everything.
          • 
          
        • One radius and one soft shadow on every element.
          • 
          
        • Reflexive glassmorphism and neon glow.
          • 
          
        • Home-made icons: improvised SVG paths or mixed icon sets instead of one library.
          • 
          
        • Emoji as icons.
          • 
          
        • Placeholder names and invented stats ("John Doe", "Acme", "+312%").
          • 
          
        • Untouched component-library defaults.
          • 
          
        • Low contrast, the most common accessibility failure in generated UI.
          • 
        
        
        
        A 5-step workflow
          
          
        1. Finish a build here and copy the master prompt. Attach one or two reference screenshots if you have them.
          2. 
          
        2. Run the design-system prompt to get the token sheet. Edit anything you disagree with before moving on.
          3. 
          
        3. Apply it to one screen at a time, including empty, loading and error states.
          4. 
          
        4. Screenshot loop: screenshot the result, compare it to the reference or token sheet, and list differences before fixing.
          5. 
          
        5. Run the audit prompt, then test the five tasks with real people. Check keyboard and screen-reader use yourself.
          6. 
        
        
      
        
      
        Several styles here use things from the list on purpose, such as glass, glow or gradients. The tell is reaching for them by default; chosen deliberately and kept legible, they are a style.
        
      
        Many of the findings on AI-generated UI come from sources that also sell design tools, so treat them as informed opinion. NN/G and the academic papers are the most independent. The workflow and the style system are my synthesis, not a published method.
